113.title: Watching change
113.hook: steps thirteen to sixteen: impermanence, fading, ceasing, letting go
113.howItsDone: In Buddhist breath meditation, the final steps turn attention to impermanence, the fading of attachment, ending and letting go, and many teachers use the breath's endings as the doorway.

segments.voice: Yesterday: citta, the mind known, gladdened, steadied and set free. Your line: release. Today, the last four steps.

Try something. Listen to the next sound you hear: a car, a fridge, a bird. Listen until it stops, and notice the exact moment it ends. Strange, isn't it? Almost all attention goes to things starting: the new message, the next episode, the plan for tomorrow. Almost none goes to things ending. But everything ends. Every sound, every mood, every breath. The last four steps of the breathing discourse turn the whole practice toward that plain fact, and say it's where freedom is found.
screen: `LISTEN UNTIL THE SOUND STOPS.` → `ALL EYES ON THE START.` → `EVERYTHING ENDS.`

segments.voice: The fourth group of four is about seeing things as they really are. Step thirteen: contemplating impermanence, anicca, I will breathe in and out. Fourteen: contemplating fading away. Fifteen: contemplating ceasing. Sixteen: contemplating letting go, relinquishment. Each goes a little deeper. Impermanence is the plain observation: this breath is changing. It started, it's moving, it's ending. Fading is seeing that as things change, the pull they have on you can fade too. Ceasing is watching things actually end: the breath, the sound, the thought, gone. And letting go is the hand opening, not because you're forced to, but because there's nothing left to cling to. The breath is the perfect teacher here. No in-breath lasts. No out-breath can be kept. You can't save a breath for later. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in four words: "All created things perish." It goes on to say that whoever sees this clearly grows weary of pain, and that this is the way to purity. That sounds bleak to some ears, but practitioners describe the opposite. When you really see that everything changes, you stop gripping so hard, and something relaxes. The bad day will end. The good day will end too, which is a reason to taste it while it's here. Every breath becomes both a beginning and an ending. The sixteen steps start with a long breath and end with letting go, and the discourse says breathing practiced this way, all the way through, brings clear knowing and release.
screen: `IMPERMANENCE: THIS BREATH IS CHANGING.` · `FADING: THE PULL FADES TOO.` · `CEASING: WATCH IT END.` · `LETTING GO: THE HAND OPENS.` · then, large: `LET GO.`

segments.voice: Rest your attention on endings: the small turn at the top of each in-breath, the pause at the bottom of each out-breath. Then widen to sounds ending, sensations fading, thoughts dissolving, with nothing to do but watch things finish. On each out-breath, let something go: a bit of tension, a thought, the need to hold on.
Watching change. The last four steps: impermanence, fading, ceasing, and letting go.
Your line: let go. The breath shows how, every time it ends. Day one hundred and thirteen, rest well.

114.title: Counting
114.hook: an old method: count breaths from one to ten, then begin again
114.howItsDone: Counting breaths from one to ten is a beginner's method described in the Visuddhimagga and also used by some Zen and Tibetan teachers, with the instruction to begin again at one whenever the count is lost.

segments.voice: Yesterday: watching change, impermanence, fading, ceasing, letting go. Your line: let go.

Sometimes it goes like this. You sit down to watch the breath. Three breaths in, you're planning dinner. Then you're rehearsing an argument. Then you're wondering if you left the stove on. Five minutes later you remember: oh, right, the breath. Sixteen beautiful steps are no use if you can't stay for two. So the old teachers gave beginners something simpler to hold on to, something any child can do. They count.
screen: `THREE BREATHS, THEN DINNER PLANS.` → `OH, RIGHT, THE BREATH.` → `SOMETHING SIMPLER: COUNT.`

segments.voice: The Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, describes counting, ganana, as the very first stage of breath meditation for a beginner. Breathe in, breathe out: one. Breathe in, breathe out: two. Up to ten, then back to one. And if you lose count, which you will, you also go back to one. The manual is oddly specific about the numbers: don't stop below five, and don't go beyond ten. Count only to three or four, and the mind feels cramped and restless, like cattle shut in a pen that's too small. Count past ten, and the mind starts paying attention to the numbers instead of the breath. Five to ten is the sweet spot: long enough to settle, short enough to stay with. Once the mind can stay with the breath without the counting, the manual says, you let the counting go. It's scaffolding, not the building. And counting isn't found only in this one manual; some Zen and Tibetan teachers count breaths with beginners too. Here's the part that matters most. Losing count isn't failure. It's the practice. Every time you notice you've drifted off to dinner plans and go back to one, that noticing is the muscle getting stronger. Reaching ten isn't the goal, and missing it isn't a mark against you. Whatever happens, the instruction stays the same, with no scolding at all.

segments.voice: Let the breath be natural, and after each out-breath count silently, one, two, up to ten, then begin again at one. If you lose track, or catch yourself at fourteen, just smile and go back to one; try for three rounds if time allows, and if you only reach three, that's fine too. The counting is a handrail: keep one hand on it.
Counting. An old method for a wandering mind: count breaths from one to ten, and begin again.
Your line: back to one. One is always there to come back to. Day one hundred and fourteen, in the books.

115.title: The hindrances arrive
115.hook: desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, doubt: five visitors every sitter meets
115.howItsDone: Buddhist meditators learn to recognize the five hindrances when they arise, noting their presence or absence, as the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness describes, before applying any remedy.

segments.voice: Yesterday: counting, one to ten, and back to one. Your line: back to one.

A sudden craving for something sweet. A flash of irritation at the neighbor's music. A heavy, sleepy fog. A restless itch to get up and check something. And a quiet voice asking: is this even working? Sit with the breath for a while and some of these may show up. Meeting them doesn't mean you're doing it wrong. The Pali texts list all five, side by side, and give them one name.
screen: `A CRAVING. A FLASH OF IRRITATION.` → `FOG. ITCH. IS THIS WORKING?` → `FIVE VISITORS, ONE NAME.`

segments.voice: That name is nivarana, a hindrance: something that blocks the view. One: sensual desire, wanting pleasant things. Two: ill will, irritation, aversion. Three: sloth and torpor, the heavy, dull, sleepy mind. Four: restlessness and worry, the buzzing mind that can't settle, and the nagging regret. Five: doubt, the wobbling mind that can't commit. In a discourse in the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha gives a picture for each, using a bowl of water you're trying to see your face in. Desire is water mixed with dye: everything gets tinted. Ill will is water boiling. Dullness is water covered in moss. Restlessness is water whipped up by the wind. Doubt is muddy water set in the dark. Each time, you can't see your reflection clearly. But the water itself is fine. It's what's in it, for now. The first thing the tradition teaches about the hindrances is simply to recognize them. In the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, when sensual desire is present, the meditator knows: sensual desire is present. When it's absent, they know it's absent. Before any remedy, you name it. Why does that help? Because a visitor you've named is no longer running the house. Restlessness you've noticed is just restlessness. Restlessness you haven't noticed becomes you, getting up to check your phone. So think of the hindrances as visitors, not enemies. They knock, they come in, they eventually leave. Your job is to see who's here.
screen: `NIVARANA: WHAT BLOCKS THE VIEW.` · `FIVE VISITORS, FROM DESIRE TO DOUBT.` · `DYED, BOILING, MOSSY, WINDY, MUDDY.` · `FIRST, JUST NAME IT.` · then, large: `NAME THE VISITOR.`

segments.voice: Each time the mind wanders, before coming back to the breath, ask which visitor this is, wanting, irritation, dullness, restlessness or doubt, and name it softly: ah, restlessness. If none is here, notice that too: no restlessness now. Don't fight them and don't feed them; just see who's here, and come back.
Nivarana. A hindrance, something that blocks the view: the five visitors a sitter meets.
Your line: name the visitor. Under the dye and the mud, the water itself is fine. Day one hundred and fifteen, complete.

116.title: Your sitting
116.hook: bell, posture, breath, a closing wish of metta
116.howItsDone: A daily sitting can take this shape: a bell or clear start, an upright posture, a breath practice, and a closing wish of loving-kindness or dedication of merit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nivarana: the five hindrances, visitors every sitter meets. Your line was name the visitor. Today is the last day with the breath.

Tomorrow morning there's no app, no teacher, nothing but a place to sit. What do you actually do? For twenty days you've learned pieces: the four phrases, the sixteen steps, counting, the visitors. What helps now is something simple and repeatable, ten minutes or twenty, done most days. Not a performance. Not a test. Just a habit with a shape to it. Today, you build yours.
screen: `TWENTY DAYS OF PIECES.` → `PUT THEM TOGETHER.` → `A HABIT WITH A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Here's a simple shape in four parts, drawn from the breathing discourse and from ordinary practice. First, a bell, or any clear beginning. In a monastery a bell or gong may open the sitting; it marks the line between the rest of your day and this. A phone timer works fine. Second, posture. The breathing discourse says: sit down, fold the legs crosswise, set the body upright. That's the old ideal; chairs and cushions both work. What matters is upright without stiffness: a straight back, relaxed shoulders, hands resting, eyes closed or softly lowered. Third, the breath. Count to ten if the mind is busy. Know the long and the short. Feel the whole body, kaya. When a visitor comes, name it, and come back. Don't try all sixteen steps at once; pick one and stay with it. Fourth, close with a wish of metta. Before you open your eyes, offer the phrases: to yourself, to someone you love, to everyone. May all beings be at ease. Some Buddhists end a sitting this way, sharing whatever good came of it outward. Then the bell again, and back to your day. How long? Ten minutes is a real sitting, and ten minutes on most days builds what an hour once a month can't: a habit. Look at the ten days behind you: sixteen steps, long and short, the whole body, joy and ease, the weather of the mind, gladdening, change, counting, the visitors, and now your own sitting. Ten minutes, yours.
screen: `A BELL: THE LINE BETWEEN.` · `UPRIGHT, NOT STIFF.` · `ONE STEP OF THE BREATH.` · `CLOSE WITH METTA.` · then, large: `TEN MINUTES, YOURS.`

segments.voice: The bell has just rung: that's your beginning. Set your posture, upright, shoulders soft, hands resting, and take one step of the breath, counting, long and short, or the whole body; when a visitor comes, name it and return. Near the end, offer the phrases: may I be at ease, may all beings be at ease.
Your sitting. Bell, posture, breath, and a closing wish of metta: a practice you can keep.

117.title: The lane
117.hook: monks walk a straight path of twenty or thirty paces, back and forth
117.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, monks and nuns practice walking meditation on a straight path, often twenty to thirty paces long, walking slowly back and forth, sometimes alternating with sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your sitting: bell, posture, breath, and a closing wish. Your line was ten minutes, yours. Today, the practice stands up.

To the car. To the kitchen. To the meeting you're late for. Ordinary walking is about the destination; the walk itself is dead time, filled with a phone or a podcast. Now a forest monastery in Thailand at dusk. Between the trees runs a narrow, swept path of sand, maybe twenty or thirty steps long. A monk walks slowly to the end, stops, turns, and walks back. And again. For an hour. He's not going anywhere. That's the point.
screen: `WALKING IS ABOUT THE DESTINATION.` → `A SWEPT PATH BETWEEN THE TREES.` → `GOING NOWHERE, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is cankama: the walking path, and the practice of walking up and down on it. It's old. In the Pali texts the Buddha is often found walking up and down in the open air, sometimes late into the night, and monks go to find him on his walking path. The monastic rules describe walking paths and even covered walking halls, so monks could practice in the rain. At Bodh Gaya, tradition marks a spot where the Buddha is said to have walked back and forth in the weeks after his awakening. Why a straight lane, and why so short? Because a lane removes the destination. On a real walk the mind is always leaning ahead: the corner, the car, the next thing. On twenty or thirty paces there's nothing ahead but the end of the lane, and then you turn around. With no errand, the mind can finally settle into the walking itself: the feel of the foot, the shift of weight, the ground. Walking meditation is sometimes treated as the lesser cousin of sitting, but teachers give it reasons of its own. It's easier when you're sleepy. It helps when the body is restless. And it's a bridge: you can't sit cross-legged in a grocery store, but you can walk with attention anywhere. In forest monasteries a monk may walk his lane for hours. For the next six days, you'll learn to walk like this. Today, just the lane. Nowhere to get to.
screen: `CANKAMA: THE WALKING PATH.` · `THE BUDDHA WALKING UP AND DOWN.` · `A LANE REMOVES THE DESTINATION.` · `A BRIDGE TO EVERYDAY LIFE.` · then, large: `NOWHERE TO GET TO.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand at one end of a few paces of floor, a hallway or a quiet corner, feel your feet on the ground, and let your hands rest in front or behind you. Walk slowly to the other end, stop for a breath, turn, and walk back, eyes lowered a few steps ahead; when the mind runs off, feel the next step. If you can't stand, feel your feet on the floor from your chair.
Cankama. The walking path, and the practice of walking back and forth on it with attention.
Your line: nowhere to get to. The lane is short on purpose. That's day one hundred seventeen.

118.title: Lifting, moving, placing
118.hook: three parts of a step, named softly
118.howItsDone: In the Burmese noting tradition of Mahasi Sayadaw, meditators walk slowly, silently labeling each part of the step, lifting, moving, placing; other traditions walk with attention but without labels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cankama: the lane, twenty or thirty paces, back and forth. Your line was nowhere to get to. Today, what's inside a single step.

Quick question: when your foot leaves the ground, which part leaves first, the heel or the toes? When it comes down, which part lands first? If you have to stand up and check, that's the point. A movement done countless times stops being felt at all. A step has become one blurry thing: walk. Today's practice slows the blur down until you can see the parts inside it, and gives each part a name.
screen: `WHICH PART LEAVES FIRST?` → `WHICH PART LANDS FIRST?` → `SLOW THE BLUR DOWN.`

segments.voice: The three-word method comes from Burma, from the teacher Mahasi Sayadaw and his students. Their walking practice uses soft mental labels, called noting. At first you note just: left, right. As attention sharpens, you break each step into parts. Lifting: the heel rises, the foot comes up. Moving: the foot swings forward through the air. Placing: the foot comes down and touches the ground. You say the words silently, lightly, at the same moment as the movement. Not before, not after. The labels are like a flashlight, keeping attention on exactly what's happening. Slow down this much and people discover that a step is not one thing. Lifting has its own feel, a lightness. Moving has a floating quality. Placing has the pressure, the contact, the weight coming back. Each part begins and ends: the impermanence you met in the breath, now in your feet. Taking a step apart isn't new. The Visuddhimagga, the old manual you met with counting, analyzes a single step into six parts, from lifting through to pressing down, and says each part arises and passes away in its own moment. Mahasi's three labels are a simpler doorway into the same observation. Some teachers use noting; others, in the Thai forest tradition for instance, simply feel the steps without words, or use a quiet word like Buddho. Different schools, the same attention. And it's slow, much slower than feels normal. That's fine. Lift, move, place.
screen: `MAHASI SAYADAW'S NOTING.` · `LIFTING, MOVING, PLACING.` · `A STEP IS NOT ONE THING.` · `SIX PARTS IN THE OLD MANUAL.` · then, large: `LIFT, MOVE, PLACE.`

segments.voice: Stand at one end of your lane, or any few paces of floor, feel the weight in both feet, and begin very slowly: as the heel rises, silently, lifting; as the foot travels forward, moving; as it touches down, placing; then the other foot. Keep the words soft, a whisper in the mind matching the movement exactly, and if the mind wanders, stop, stand, feel the feet, and begin again. If you can't stand, lift and place one foot while seated.
Lifting. The first of three parts of a step, named softly: lifting, moving, placing.
Your line: lift, move, place. A step is not one thing. Day one hundred eighteen, done.

119.title: The turn
119.hook: the turn at the end of the lane is its own practice
119.howItsDone: In the noting style of walking meditation, meditators pause at the end of the lane, note standing and the intention to turn, and turn slowly with full attention before walking back.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lifting: a step taken apart and named softly. Your line was lift, move, place. Today, the end of the week.

Walking from the car to the door. Waiting for the kettle. The half-second between finishing one email and opening the next. In-between moments, easy to treat as nothing. That's exactly where attention leaks away. On the walking lane, the in-between moment is the turn: you reach the end, and there's a little gap before you walk back. It's easy to rush it. Swing around, done. But teachers keep saying the same surprising thing: the turn is its own practice.
screen: `THE IN-BETWEEN MOMENTS.` → `WHERE ATTENTION LEAKS AWAY.` → `THE TURN IS ITS OWN PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: In the Burmese noting method, the turn has its own labels. You reach the end of the lane. Standing, standing: you stop and feel the whole body, kaya, upright. Then something easy to miss: intending to turn. Before the body moves there's an intention, a tiny decision, and the practice asks you to catch it. Then turning, turning, as the body slowly rotates, one foot at a time. Then standing again, intending to walk, and off you go. Why so much fuss about a turn? Because it's where the mind likes to wake up and wander off. Walking in a straight line, attention can settle into a rhythm. At the turn the rhythm breaks, and the mind jumps to the next thing. If you can stay present through the turn, you can stay present through the bigger turns of the day: getting up, sitting down, walking into a room, starting a new task. Catching the intention matters in Buddhist teaching generally. Intention, cetana, is what the Buddha pointed to as the heart of action. Noticing the small intention before a turn is practice for noticing the bigger ones before you speak or act. And look back at this week: watching change, counting, the visitors, your own sitting, the lane, the parts of a step, and now the turn. Seven days that carried the practice from the breath to the feet. The turn counts too, and so do all the in-between moments.
screen: `STANDING, STANDING.` · `INTENDING TO TURN.` · `TURNING, TURNING.` · `THE BIGGER TURNS OF THE DAY.` · then, large: `THE TURN COUNTS TOO.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly to the end of your few paces of floor, stop, feel yourself standing, and notice the wish to turn before you move. Turn slowly, one small step at a time, feeling the feet shift and the body rotate; stand for a breath, notice the wish to walk, and walk back, letting each turn be as careful as each step. If you're seated, turn your head slowly, noticing the intention first.
The turn. The moment at the end of the lane: standing, intending, turning, a practice of its own.
Your line: the turn counts too. Before the body moves, there's a choice. That's a week, from the breath to the feet.

chat.says: Why would walking meditation make such a fuss about turning around?
options: The turn breaks the rhythm, so the mind wanders there; staying present trains you for life's turns.
Turning quickly keeps the walk smooth, so the turn is meant to be rushed through.
The turn is the rest break, the one moment you're free to let the mind wander.
chat.meaning: At the turn the rhythm breaks and the mind jumps ahead. Staying present there, intention first, trains you for the day's bigger turns.
